claim: Treatment of EGFR-mutant lung cancer with erlotinib results in dramatic tumor regression but it is invariably followed by drug resistance.
source: Treatment of EGFR-mutant lung cancer with erlotinib results in dramatic tumor regression but it is invariably followed by drug resistance.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical observation cited in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: SOX2 is rapidly and specifically induced following erlotinib treatment of mutant EGFR-addicted cells, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: In characterizing early transcriptional changes following drug treatment of mutant EGFR-addicted cells, we identified the stem cell transcriptional regulator SOX2 as being rapidly and specifically induced, both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from microarray analysis, qPCR, immunofluorescence, and xenograft studies shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Suppression of SOX2 sensitizes cells to erlotinib-mediated apoptosis.
source: Suppression of SOX2 sensitizes cells to erlotinib-mediated apoptosis, ultimately decreasing the emergence of acquired resistance, whereas its ectopic expression reduces drug-induced cell death.
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5B,D and ectopic expression experiments in Figure 5A.

claim: Ectopic expression of SOX2 reduces erlotinib-induced cell death.
source: Suppression of SOX2 sensitizes cells to erlotinib-mediated apoptosis, ultimately decreasing the emergence of acquired resistance, whereas its ectopic expression reduces drug-induced cell death.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5A showing decreased PARP and caspase-3 cleavage with ectopic SOX2 expression.

claim: Erlotinib relieves EGFR-dependent suppression of FOXO6.
source: We show that erlotinib relieves EGFR-dependent suppression of FOXO6, leading to its induction of SOX2, which in turn represses the pro-apoptotic BH3-only genes BIM and BMF.
evidence: This is supported by data showing FOXO6 knockdown blocks SOX2 induction (Figure 7) and loss of AKT-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation of FOXO proteins (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).

claim: FOXO6 induces SOX2 expression following erlotinib treatment.
source: We show that erlotinib relieves EGFR-dependent suppression of FOXO6, leading to its induction of SOX2, which in turn represses the pro-apoptotic BH3-only genes BIM and BMF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments in Figure 7B,C,D showing that FOXO6 knockdown blocks SOX2 induction.

claim: SOX2 represses the pro-apoptotic BH3-only genes BIM and BMF.
source: We show that erlotinib relieves EGFR-dependent suppression of FOXO6, leading to its induction of SOX2, which in turn represses the pro-apoptotic BH3-only genes BIM and BMF.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing SOX2 binding to BIM and BMF promoters (Figure 6B) and qPCR data showing reduced BIM and BMF induction with ectopic SOX2 (Figure 6A).

claim: The T790M 'gatekeeper' mutation within the EGFR kinase domain restores ATP binding in the presence of erlotinib.
source: Following dramatic initial tumor shrinkage, tumor regrowth is most frequently associated with the emergence of a secondary genetic change, the T790M 'gatekeeper' mutation within the EGFR kinase domain, which restores ATP binding in the presence of drug (Pao et al., 2004; Kobayashi et al., 2005; Yun et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Amplification of MET or mutational activation of downstream kinases (BRAF, PIK3CA) may bypass the effect of EGFR inhibition.
source: In other cases, amplification of related receptor tyrosine kinases (e.g., MET) or mutational activation of downstream kinases (e.g., BRAF, PIK3CA) may bypass the effect of EGFR inhibition (Engelman et al., 2007; Sequist et al., 2011; Ohashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Clinical trials involving rebiopsy of tumor lesions at the earliest sign of drug resistance have revealed phenotypic conversions including activation of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and trans-differentiation of lung cancers from adenocarcinoma to small cell histologies.
source: Recently, clinical trials involving rebiopsy of tumor lesions at the earliest sign of drug resistance have also revealed phenotypic conversions that may contribute to drug resistance, including activation of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and the remarkable trans-differentiation of lung cancers from adenocarcinoma to small cell histologies (Thomson et al., 2005; Witta et al., 2006; Sequist et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A transient 'drug-tolerant' state may precede the development of mutationally defined, heritable drug resistance.
source: In vitro modeling of acquired resistance to EGFR inhibitors has raised the possibility that a transient so-called 'drug-tolerant' state may precede the development of mutationally defined, heritable drug resistance (Sharma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: In PC9 mutant, EGFR-addicted lung cancer cells, EGFR inhibition triggers apoptosis in the vast majority of cells in vitro, uncovering approximately 0.3% that are drug tolerant, quiescent, and expressing the stem cell marker CD133 and the histone H3K4 demethylase KDM5A.
source: In PC9 mutant, EGFR-addicted lung cancer cells, EGFR inhibition triggers apoptosis in the vast majority of cells in vitro, uncovering approximately 0.3% that are drug tolerant, quiescent, and expressing the stem cell marker CD133 and the histone H3K4 demethylase KDM5A (Sharma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Acute loss of ERK signaling triggered by RAF or MEK inhibitors in BRAF mutant melanoma cells relieves ERK-dependent inhibition of RAS and CRAF, whose activation through ErbB receptor signaling may lead to paradoxical proliferative signals.
source: For instance, acute loss of ERK signaling triggered by RAF or MEK inhibitors in BRAF mutant melanoma cells relieves ERK-dependent inhibition of RAS and CRAF, whose activation through ErbB receptor signaling may lead to paradoxical proliferative signals (Pratilas et al., 2009; Paraiso et al., 2010; Lito et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: In BRAF mutant colorectal cancers, feedback activation of EGFR-dependent signaling attenuates the consequences of mutant BRAF inhibition, suppressing the apoptotic effect.
source: Similarly, in BRAF mutant colorectal cancers, feedback activation of EGFR-dependent signaling attenuates the consequences of mutant BRAF inhibition, suppressing the apoptotic effect (Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: A total of 35 genes showed >fourfold change in expression (FDR <0.05) in HCC827 cells treated with erlotinib for 6 hr, including 22 downregulated and 13 upregulated transcripts.
source: A total of 35 genes showed >fourfold change in expression (FDR <0.05), including 22 downregulated and 13 upregulated transcripts (represented by 48 unique probe sets; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SOX2 was strongly induced in three mutant EGFR-addicted lung cancer cell lines (HCC827, PC9, H3255) following treatment with physiologically relevant concentrations of erlotinib (0.1 µM).
source: Thus, SOX2 was strongly induced in three mutant EGFR-addicted lung cancer cell lines (HCC827, PC9, H3255) following treatment with physiologically relevant concentrations of erlotinib (0.1 µM), but not when these cells were treated with comparably effective doses of cytotoxic chemotherapy (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: SOX2 was not induced when EGFR-mutant cells were treated with comparably effective doses of cytotoxic chemotherapy.
source: Thus, SOX2 was strongly induced in three mutant EGFR-addicted lung cancer cell lines (HCC827, PC9, H3255) following treatment with physiologically relevant concentrations of erlotinib (0.1 µM), but not when these cells were treated with comparably effective doses of cytotoxic chemotherapy (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SOX2 was not induced in ALK-translocated lung cancer cells treated with crizotinib, HER2-amplified breast cancer cells exposed to lapatinib or BRAF-mutant melanoma cells treated with AZD6244.
source: SOX2 was also not induced in other oncogene-dependent models, such as ALK-translocated lung cancer cells treated with crizotinib, HER2-amplified breast cancer cells exposed to lapatinib or BRAF-mutant melanoma cells treated with AZD6244 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: SOX2 was not induced following erlotinib treatment of H1975 cells, which harbor both an EGFR activating mutation and the T790M gatekeeper mutation that confers resistance to erlotinib.
source: Consistent with its dependence on suppression of mutant EGFR signaling in the context of EGFR 'addiction', SOX2 was not induced following erlotinib treatment of H1975 cells, which harbor both an EGFR activating mutation and the T790M gatekeeper mutation that confers resistant to erlotinib; or in H1650 cells with mutated EGFR that are relatively resistant to the effects of EGFR inhibition in part through genetic loss of PTEN (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) (Sos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Treatment of H1975 cells with the L858R/T790M mutation-selective inhibitor WZ4002 resulted in SOX2 induction.
source: However, treatment of H1975 cells with the L858R/T790M mutation-selective inhibitor WZ4002 resulted in SOX2 induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, right) (Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and citation to prior literature.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of EGFR led to strong induction of SOX2 in cells that show erlotinib-mediated induction of SOX2.
source: In cells that show erlotinib-mediated induction of SOX2, siRNA-mediated knockdown of EGFR also led to strong induction of SOX2 (in the absence of erlotinib), confirming the specificity of the drug effect (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Simultaneous treatment of cells with actinomycin D and erlotinib suppressed the induction of SOX2, consistent with a primary effect of EGFR inhibition in increasing SOX2 transcript levels.
source: Simultaneous treatment of cells with actinomycin D and erlotinib suppressed the induction of SOX2, consistent with a primary effect of EGFR inhibition in increasing SOX2 transcript levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: SOX2 expression following exposure of HCC827 cells to erlotinib was transient, peaking at 24 hr after exposure to therapeutic levels of the drug.
source: Remarkably, SOX2 expression following exposure of HCC827 cells to erlotinib was transient, peaking at 24 hr after exposure to therapeutic levels of the drug (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SOX2 expression returned to basal levels despite continued erlotinib treatment in surviving cells.
source: Thereafter, SOX2 expression returned to basal levels despite continued erlotinib treatment in surviving cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D and immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: SOX2 encodes a master transcriptional regulator, implicated in stem cell maintenance and iPS cell generation.
source: SOX2 encodes a master transcriptional regulator, implicated in stem cell maintenance and iPS cell generation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SOX2 function.

claim: SOX2 is required for upper aerodigestive tract development.
source: It is also required for upper aerodigestive tract development, and is known to be amplified in a subset of esophageal and squamous lung cancers, although it has not been previously implicated in lung adenocarcinomas, including the subset driven by mutant EGFR (Ellis et al., 2004; Gontan et al., 2008; Bass et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SOX2 is known to be amplified in a subset of esophageal and squamous lung cancers.
source: It is also required for upper aerodigestive tract development, and is known to be amplified in a subset of esophageal and squamous lung cancers, although it has not been previously implicated in lung adenocarcinomas, including the subset driven by mutant EGFR (Ellis et al., 2004; Gontan et al., 2008; Bass et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SOX2 has not been previously implicated in lung adenocarcinomas, including the subset driven by mutant EGFR.
source: It is also required for upper aerodigestive tract development, and is known to be amplified in a subset of esophageal and squamous lung cancers, although it has not been previously implicated in lung adenocarcinomas, including the subset driven by mutant EGFR (Ellis et al., 2004; Gontan et al., 2008; Bass et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The level of SOX2 induction in cultured cells exposed to erlotinib showed considerable heterogeneity, with a subset of cells (~20%) expressing high levels.
source: The level of SOX2 induction in cultured cells exposed to erlotinib showed considerable heterogeneity, with a subset of cells (∼20%, with some experimental variability) expressing high levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The SOX2+ fraction was not increased by higher drug dosage, beyond that required for full inhibition of EGFR.
source: The SOX2+ fraction was not increased by higher drug dosage, beyond that required for full inhibition of EGFR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SOX2 expression did not correlate with expression of the putative stem cell markers CD133, CD44, CD24, OCT-4, or KLF-4.
source: However, SOX2 expression did not correlate with expression of the putative stem cell markers CD133, CD44, CD24, OCT-4, or KLF-4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) nor did microarray-based expression profiling of high SOX2-sorted cells identify a stem-like signature (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: SOX2-expressing cells had a very low proliferative index, as measured by Ki67 staining (0.5% of Ki67+/SOX2+ vs 51% Ki67+/SOX2− HCC827 cells at baseline [p = 0.015]; and 0.15% Ki67+/SOX2+ vs 6.4% Ki67+/SOX2− cells following erlotinib [p < 0.0001]).
source: Nonetheless, SOX2-expressing cells had a very low proliferative index, as measured by Ki67 staining (0.5% of Ki67+/SOX2+ vs 51% Ki67+/SOX2− HCC827 cells at baseline [p = 0.015]; and 0.15% Ki67+/SOX2+ vs 6.4% Ki67+/SOX2− cells following erlotinib [p < 0.0001]) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Retreatment of cells after a period of recovery produced similar heterogeneity of SOX2+ cells as the initial treatment, pointing to the absence of enrichment for highly inducible cells.
source: Retreatment of cells after a period of recovery produced similar heterogeneity of SOX2+ cells as the initial treatment, pointing to the absence of enrichment for highly inducible cells (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: SOX2 could still be induced in cells made resistant to erlotinib, but only at the much higher doses of drug required to fully inhibit EGFR in resistant cells.
source: In addition, SOX2 could still be induced in cells made resistant to erlotinib, but only at the much higher doses of drug required to fully inhibit EGFR in resistant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Cloning of 5–6 individual HCC827 and PC9 cells consistently generated mixed populations, including high level SOX2 inducers together with non-expressing cells, demonstrating that this heterogeneity is likely stochastic, rather than heritable.
source: Finally, cloning of 5–6 individual HCC827 and PC9 cells consistently generated mixed populations, including high level SOX2 inducers together with non-expressing cells, demonstrating that this heterogeneity is likely stochastic, rather than heritable (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed minimal SOX2 expression in mock-treated PC9 xenografts (mean 0.2 SOX2+ nuclei per field), but clearly increased (and heterogeneous) SOX2 positive cells after a single dose of erlotinib (mean: 7.4 SOX2+ nuclei per field, N = 147–151 fields, p < 0.0001).
source: Immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis revealed minimal SOX2 expression in mock-treated xenografts (mean 0.2 SOX2+ nuclei per field), but clearly increased (and heterogeneous) SOX2 positive cells after a single dose of erlotinib (mean: 7.4 SOX2+ nuclei per field, N = 147–151 fields, p < 0.0001) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In HCC827 cell-derived xenografts, a single oral dose of erlotinib increased both the number of SOX2-positive cells and the level of SOX2 expression per nucleus.
source: Similar studies in HCC827 cell-derived xenografts revealed low (but detectable) levels of SOX2 expression in mock-treated tumors; again, a single oral dose of erlotinib increased both the number of SOX2-positive cells and the level of SOX2 expression per nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SOX2 induction was absent following treatment of patient-derived EGFR-mutant cells with erlotinib, which was ineffective in inhibiting EGFR in these resistant patient-derived cells.
source: SOX2 induction was absent following treatment with erlotinib, which was ineffective in inhibiting EGFR in these resistant patient-derived cells (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR, immunofluorescence, and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The novel 'third line' irreversible, EGFR-mutant-specific inhibitor WZ4002 demonstrated potent EGFR inhibition in patient-derived cells with T790M mutation, along with induction of SOX2.
source: However, the novel 'third line' irreversible, EGFR-mutant-specific inhibitor WZ4002 demonstrated potent EGFR inhibition in these cells, along with induction of SOX2 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR, immunofluorescence, and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Expression of ectopic SOX2 significantly decreased erlotinib-mediated apoptosis, resulting in decreased PARP and caspase-3 cleavage.
source: In contrast, expression of ectopic SOX2 significantly decreased erlotinib-mediated apoptosis, resulting in decreased PARP and caspase-3 cleavage (Figure 5A, lane 2 vs 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Exogenous SOX2 itself did not alter basal or erlotinib-inhibited phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, or ERK.
source: Exogenous SOX2 itself did not alter basal or erlotinib-inhibited phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, or ERK (Figure 5A, lanes 3–4).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SOX2 knockdown further increased erlotinib-induced apoptosis in HCC827 and PC9 cells, as determined by PARP and caspase-3 cleavage assays and by cell enumeration.
source: While both HCC827 and PC9 cells are highly sensitive to EGFR inhibition at baseline, SOX2 knockdown further increased erlotinib-induced apoptosis, as determined by PARP and caspase-3 cleavage assays and by cell enumeration (Figure 5B,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5B and toxicity assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: The apoptotic effect of the most potent siRNA was rescued by expression of an ectopic siRNA-resistant SOX2 construct.
source: The apoptotic effect of the most potent siRNA was rescued by expression of an ectopic siRNA-resistant SOX2 construct (Figure 5C) and individual siRNAs-induced apoptosis in proportion to the degree of knockdown (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), confirming the specificity of the effect.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Endogenous SOX2 suppression itself did not have a consistent effect on EGFR signaling, as measured by phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, or ERK.
source: As with expression of exogenous SOX2, endogenous SOX2 suppression itself did not have a consistent effect on EGFR signaling, as measured by phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, or ERK (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Preventing the short-term induction of SOX2 using siRNA allows fewer cells to survive the initial exposure to erlotinib, preventing an adaptation response that ultimately delays the emergence of erlotinib-resistant colonies.
source: Consistent with the short-term duration of siRNA effectiveness, these results suggest that preventing the short-term induction of SOX2 allows fewer cells to survive the initial exposure to erlotinib, preventing an adaptation response that ultimately delays the emergence of erlotinib-resistant colonies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating decreased colony formation with SOX2 knockdown.

claim: Three of 14 BH3-domain containing proteins tested showed strongly reduced mRNA induction by erlotinib in the presence of ectopic SOX2: BIM, BMF, and HRK (but not PUMA).
source: In both HCC827 and PC9 EGFR-mutant lung cancer cells, three of 14 BH3-domain containing proteins tested showed strongly reduced mRNA induction by erlotinib in the presence of ectopic SOX2: BIM, BMF, and HRK (but not PUMA) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strong SOX2-binding peaks were present within ~2 kB of the transcriptional start sites (TSS) of both BIM and BMF genes.
source: Strong SOX2-binding peaks were present within ∼2 kB of the transcriptional start sites (TSS) of both BIM and BMF genes (for BMF, the peak spans the TSS; for BIM, it is located within the first intron) (Figure 6B, upper).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ChIP qPCR demonstrated significant enhancement of SOX2 binding with erlotinib treatment at both BIM and BMF peaks compared to untreated cells.
source: Importantly, ChIP qPCR demonstrated significant enhancement of SOX2 binding with erlotinib treatment at both peaks compared to untreated cells, suggesting that binding is functionally significant (Figure 6B, lower).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of either BIM or BMF (but not HRK) decreased erlotinib-induced apoptosis, with combined BIM and BMF knockdown displaying an additive effect.
source: Consistent with their functional roles, knockdown of either BIM or BMF (but not HRK) decreased erlotinib-induced apoptosis, with combined BIM and BMF knockdown displaying an additive effect (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Several binding motifs for FOXO proteins were highly significantly enriched in the promoters of the 12 highest erlotinib-induced genes (q-value = 0.003 or less).
source: To search for mediators of SOX2 induction, we explored the Molecular Signatures and TRANSFAC databases for transcription factor target sequences within the promoters of the 12 highest erlotinib-induced genes (Wingender et al., 2000; Subramanian et al., 2005). Several binding motifs for FOXO proteins were highly significantly enriched (q-value = 0.003 or less): for SOX2, multiple sites were present within 2 kb of the transcriptional start site (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of all of the FOXO family members was detectable at baseline in HCC827 cells and erlotinib treatment (8 hr) was associated with a 1.6–4.4-fold induction.
source: Expression of all of the FOXO family members was detectable at baseline in HCC827 cells and erlotinib treatment (8 hr) was associated with a 1.6–4.4-fold induction (Figure 7B), as well as with loss of the AKT-mediated inhibitory N-terminal threonine phosphorylation of the FOXO proteins (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B and immunoblot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Knockdown of FOXO6 using pooled siRNA constructs, but not the other FOXO proteins (individually or simultaneously), dramatically reduced erlotinib-mediated induction of SOX2.
source: Knockdown of FOXO6 using pooled siRNA constructs, but not the other FOXO proteins (individually or simultaneously), dramatically reduced erlotinib-mediated induction of SOX2 (Figure 7B,C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 7B and immunofluorescence data in Figure 7C.

claim: The effect of FOXO6 knockdown on SOX2 was evident using multiple individual siRNAs targeting FOXO6 in both HCC827 and PC9 cells.
source: The effect of FOXO6 knockdown on SOX2 was evident using multiple individual siRNAs targeting FOXO6 in both HCC827 and PC9 cells (Figure 7D; effect on other FOXO isoforms is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The effect of FOXO6 knockdown on SOX2 was not associated with any consistent effect on other aspects of EGFR signaling, although a moderate decrease in phospho-EGFR was observed in some experiments without significant differences in phospho-AKT or phospho-ERK.
source: The effect of FOXO6 knockdown on SOX2 was not associated with any consistent effect on other aspects of EGFR signaling, although a moderate decrease in phospho-EGFR was observed in some experiments without significant differences in phospho-AKT or phospho-ERK (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: FOXO6 expression was heterogeneous and partially colocalized with SOX2 expression among populations of both untreated and treated cells.
source: Notably, FOXO6 expression was also heterogeneous and partially colocalized with SOX2 expression among populations of both untreated and treated cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: FOXO6 differs from other FOXO proteins in that even the inactive protein is localized in the nucleus.
source: FOXO6 differs from other FOXO proteins in that even the inactive protein is localized in the nucleus (Jacobs et al., 2003; van der Heide et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The HCC2935 human lung cancer cell line harbors a characteristic oncogene-addicting EGFR mutation (exon 19 deletion) yet has unexplained resistance to erlotinib.
source: The HCC2935 human lung cancer cell line is remarkable for harboring a characteristic oncogene-addicting EGFR mutation (exon 19 deletion) yet having unexplained resistance to erlotinib (Figure 8A), including absence of the common T790M gatekeeper mutation within EGFR and no amplification of the MET bypass signaling pathway (Zheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by toxicity assay data in Figure 8A and citation to prior literature.

claim: SOX2 expression at baseline is detectable in 90% of HCC2935 cells (compared to 3% of HCC827 and <1% PC9 cells), and its expression per cell is further increased upon EGFR inhibition.
source: Notably, SOX2 expression at baseline is detectable in 90% of HCC2935 cells (compared to 3% of HCC827 and <1% PC9 cells), and its expression per cell is further increased upon EGFR inhibition (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A striking increase in erlotinib cytotoxicity was evident in HCC2935 cells following SOX2 suppression (IC50 0.8 µM for siCTRL cells with no further toxicity up to 10 µM, IC50 0.1 µM for siSOX2 cells), associated with higher levels of BIM and increased PARP and caspase-3 cleavage.
source: To test whether increased SOX2 contributes to decreased erlotinib sensitivity in HCC2935 cells, we knocked down SOX2 using siRNA. A striking increase in erlotinib cytotoxicity was evident following SOX2 suppression (IC50 0.8 µM for siCTRL cells with no further toxicity up to 10 µM, IC50 0.1 µM for siSOX2 cells), associated with higher levels of BIM and increased PARP and caspase-3 cleavage (Figure 8A,C).
evidence: This is supported by toxicity assay data in Figure 8A and immunoblot data in Figure 8C.

claim: Increased baseline SOX2 contributes to erlotinib resistance in HCC2935 EGFR-mutant cells.
source: Thus, increased baseline SOX2 contributes to erlotinib resistance in these EGFR-mutant cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 8A,C demonstrating increased erlotinib sensitivity with SOX2 knockdown.

claim: The best studied FOXO isoform, FOXO1, is highly expressed in ES cells and has been implicated in the maintenance of pluripotency through activation of SOX2 transcription.
source: The best studied isoform, FOXO1, is highly expressed in ES cells and has been implicated in the maintenance of pluripotency through activation of SOX2 transcription (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: All FOXO proteins bind to similar DNA sequences, with isoform-specific activity presumably conferred by cellular and promoter context.
source: All FOXO proteins bind to similar DNA sequences, with isoform-specific activity presumably conferred by cellular and promoter context (Furuyama et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: All four FOXO isoforms are expressed in EGFR-mutant lung cancer cells, transcriptionally induced following EGFR inhibition and phosphorylated at homologous Serine residues, yet only FOXO6 regulates SOX2 in these cells.
source: Indeed, all four FOXO isoforms are expressed in EGFR-mutant lung cancer cells, transcriptionally induced following EGFR inhibition and phosphorylated at homologous Serine residues, yet only FOXO6 regulates SOX2 in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7B,C,D showing specific effect of FOXO6 knockdown on SOX2.

claim: Treatment with PI3K inhibitors alone is insufficient for induction of SOX2.
source: Activation of FOXO6 may occur through both AKT dependent and independent pathways (Jacobs et al., 2003; van der Heide et al., 2005), and indeed we observed that treatment with PI3K inhibitors alone is insufficient for induction of SOX2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B and citations to prior literature.

claim: Other pathways that have been implicated in SOX2 regulation in the developing lung, including FGF10, WNT/beta-Catenin signaling, and TTF1, had relatively modest effects on its induction following erlotinib treatment in EGFR-mutant cancer cells.
source: Other pathways that have been implicated in SOX2 regulation in the developing lung, including FGF10, WNT/beta-Catenin signaling, and TTF1 (Que et al., 2007; Gontan et al., 2008; Hashimoto et al., 2012), had relatively modest effects on its induction following erlotinib treatment in EGFR-mutant cancer cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), pointing to FOXO6 as the dominant pathway in this model of oncogene-dependent signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 and citations to prior literature.

claim: BMF binds with significant affinity to a subset of BCL-2 family members (BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-w).
source: In contrast to the latter, BMF binds with significant affinity to a subset of BCL-2 family members (BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-w) (Chen et al., 2005; Kuwana et al., 2005), yet it clearly contributes to the apoptotic response to erlotinib (Figure 6).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The direct binding by SOX2 of the BIM and BMF genes is consistent with the ability of the four reprogramming factors (SOX2, OCT-4, KLF-4, and c-MYC) to bind to the promoters of several anti-apoptotic genes (including BMF) which are induced early during the reprogramming process.
source: The direct binding by SOX2 of the BIM and BMF genes is consistent with the ability of the four reprogramming factors (SOX2, OCT-4, KLF-4, and c-MYC) to bind to the promoters of several anti-apoptotic genes (including BMF) which are induced early during the reprogramming process (Kim et al., 2008; Soufi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In a recent study of lung cancers with wild-type EGFR, the activation of EGFR upregulated SOX2, thereby decreasing apoptosis through BCL2L1, a phenomenon that was notably absent in EGFR-mutant lung cancers.
source: Interestingly, control of SOX2 expression and its modulation of apoptosis may differ in EGFR-mutant lung cancer, compared with other forms of NSCLC. In a recent study of lung cancers with wild-type EGFR, the activation of EGFR upregulated SOX2, thereby decreasing apoptosis through BCL2L1, a phenomenon that was notably absent in EGFR-mutant lung cancers (Chou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A similar EGFR-SOX2-BCL2L1 pathway was reported in a prostate cancer cell line, also with wild-type EGFR.
source: A similar pathway was reported in a prostate cancer cell line, also with wild-type EGFR (Rybak and Tang, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: An EGFR-SOX2-BCL2L1 pathway may be implicated in cancer cells with wild-type EGFR, whereas the EGFR-FOXO6-SOX2-BIM/BMF pathway is specific for cells that are dependent on mutant EGFR signals for their survival.
source: Thus, an EGFR-SOX2-BCL2L1 pathway may be implicated in cancer cells with wild-type EGFR, whereas the EGFR-FOXO6-SOX2-BIM/BMF pathway we describe is specific for cells that are dependent on mutant EGFR signals for their survival.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of the current study's findings with prior literature.

claim: The heterogeneous induction of SOX2 within a clonally derived cell population could reflect the existence of an intrinsic subpopulation with heritable traits, as recently proposed in medulloblastoma and skin carcinoma.
source: The heterogeneous induction of SOX2 within a clonally derived cell population could reflect the existence of an intrinsic subpopulation with heritable traits, as recently proposed in medulloblastoma and skin carcinoma (Boumahdi et al., 2014; Vanner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: The heterogeneous induction of SOX2 could result from stochastic variation between cells in the activity of cellular signaling pathways.
source: Alternatively, it could result from stochastic variation between cells in the activity of cellular signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The authors favor a stochastic model for SOX2 heterogeneity, given the absent coexpression of SOX2 with putative stem cell markers, the failure to enrich for SOX2 positive cells following repeated erlotinib treatments, and the regeneration of heterogeneous SOX2 inducibility following single cell cloning experiments.
source: We favor the latter model, given the absent coexpression of SOX2 with putative stem cell markers, the failure to enrich for SOX2 positive cells following repeated erlotinib treatments, and the regeneration of heterogeneous SOX2 inducibility following single cell cloning experiments.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, 5.

claim: A stochastic cell killing model for TRAIL-induced apoptosis of HeLa cells was recently described, in which naturally occurring cell-to-cell variation in the levels or activity of upstream signaling proteins leads to differential induction of mitochondrial membrane permeability and apoptosis only in some cells.
source: A stochastic cell killing model for TRAIL-induced apoptosis of HeLa cells was recently described, in which naturally occurring cell-to-cell variation in the levels or activity of upstream signaling proteins leads to differential induction of mitochondrial membrane permeability and apoptosis only in some cells (Spencer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The ability of siRNA targeting SOX2 to substantially decrease the number and rate at which resistant subclones of EGFR-mutant cells emerge following continuous erlotinib treatment suggests that, despite its heterogeneous, transient, and stochastic expression, SOX2 contributes to the emergence of stably acquired resistance.
source: Critically, the ability of siRNA targeting SOX2 to substantially decrease the number and rate at which resistant subclones of EGFR-mutant cells emerge following continuous erlotinib treatment suggests that, despite its heterogeneous, transient, and stochastic expression, SOX2 contributes to the emergence of stably acquired resistance (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Drug-tolerant persister cells (DTPs) emerge following longer erlotinib exposure at much higher concentrations than SOX2+ cells, and they constitute a lower percentage of cells within the population.
source: However, there are also significant differences between the mechanisms underlying DTPs and those observed here. DTPs emerge following longer erlotinib exposure at much higher concentrations, and they constitute a lower percentage of cells within the population.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior literature on DTPs.

claim: The expression of the stem cell marker CD133 and the chromatin remodeling protein KDM5A by DTPs was not reproduced by SOX2+ cells.
source: Their expression of the stem cell marker CD133 and the chromatin remodeling protein KDM5A was not reproduced by SOX2+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 6.

claim: DTPs are detectable in many cancer cell lines following treatment with multiple cytotoxic and targeted agents, whereas induction of SOX2 appears to be strictly limited to targeted EGFR inhibition in cells addicted to mutant EGFR signaling.
source: Furthermore, DTPs are detectable in many cancer cell lines following treatment with multiple cytotoxic and targeted agents, whereas induction of SOX2 appears to be strictly limited to targeted EGFR inhibition in cells addicted to mutant EGFR signaling.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior literature on DTPs and data from Figure 1.

claim: SOX2 induction may be a specific and early signaling response to EGFR withdrawal, which contributes to increased cell survival, thus enhancing the likelihood of epigenetic events leading to DTPs and ultimately to stable genetic mechanisms of acquired drug resistance.
source: SOX2 induction may thus be a specific and early signaling response to EGFR withdrawal, which contributes to increased cell survival, thus enhancing the likelihood of epigenetic events leading to DTPs and ultimately to stable genetic mechanisms of acquired drug resistance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their data.

claim: In a subset of cases, high basal SOX2 may blunt the initial signaling response to EGFR inhibitors.
source: Our results with HCC2935 cells (Figure 8) further suggest that in a subset of cases, high basal SOX2 may even blunt the initial signaling response to EGFR inhibitors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of data shown in Figure 8.
